questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether an old proxy calibration may be applied to a new period
questions.stem: A transit planner's board reviews whether a proxy calibration fitted to 1990s tree-ring widths still transfers to today's river flow.

options.text: Re-estimate the calibration, because the proxy-to-climate relationship is only valid over its fitted period
Keep the old calibration unchanged, since the instrument certificate was never revoked after fitting
options.misconception: assumes paperwork proves the climate response stayed fixed

options.text: Abandon the proxy entirely, because tree rings can never represent cold-season precipitation
options.misconception: believes tree rings are useless for any precipitation record

options.text: Retain the calibration only if the sample size exceeds the length of the calibration period
options.misconception: confuses sample size with a valid calibration

questions.explanation: Stationarity means the mapping between proxy and target stays stable, and nothing guarantees that across decades. If the system or the proxy's sensitivity shifted, the old fit drifts, so re-estimating is the safe move.
questions.hint: Ask whether the old mapping still holds in the new period.

options.text: The gap is large enough that cloud contamination or sensor calibration needs checking
The difference is normal, so averaging the two passes is the appropriate next step

options.text: One pass should be discarded, since satellite retrievals never agree with ground truth
options.misconception: believes satellite and ground data can never differ

questions.explanation: A 33 mm spread over one snowfield exceeds normal retrieval uncertainty, so it signals a fault to diagnose rather than noise. Averaging would hide that fault, and neither sensor nor ground truth is automatically right.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the fluxes subtracted to obtain net radiation
questions.stem: An energy-balance diagram for a station forecourt labels incoming shortwave, reflected shortwave, outgoing longwave and latent heat; which pair is subtracted from incoming shortwave to give net radiation?

options.text: Only reflected shortwave, because longwave loss is treated as stored heat
options.misconception: ignores longwave loss when forming net radiation

options.text: Only outgoing longwave, because the surface is treated as perfectly absorbing
options.misconception: assumes zero albedo for the whole surface

options.text: Both reflected shortwave and outgoing longwave
Neither of them, because net radiation equals gross incoming shortwave by definition
options.misconception: thinks net radiation always equals gross incoming

questions.explanation: Net radiation is incoming shortwave minus reflected shortwave and outgoing longwave, leaving energy for latent, sensible and storage fluxes. Ignoring either loss term overstates the energy available.
questions.hint: Subtract reflection and emission from incoming shortwave.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Residence time in the water cycle
questions.learningObjective: Design a tracer study to estimate reservoir residence time
questions.stem: The reservoir team is asked to design a tracer study that measures how long a marked parcel of water stays in the reservoir before release.

answer.exemplar: Inject a conservative tracer, such as a measured dose of dissolved chloride or a dye, at the inlet and sample the outflow at fixed intervals to build a concentration curve. Estimate mean residence time from the tracer mass divided by the outflow rate, and check the curve shape: a long tail signals short-circuiting rather than complete mixing.

questions.explanation: A conservative tracer tracks the flow, so its recovery curve measures retention. Recovered tracer mass divided by outflow rate gives the mean residence time, and the curve shape reveals short-circuiting.
questions.hint: Use a tracer that does not react with the reservoir water.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a modelled heat island cooling may exceed the measured cooling
questions.stem: A bus corridor pilot added street trees and light paving, and the board asks why the measured cooling fell short of the modelled prediction.

answer.exemplar: The model assumed the trees were mature, so it credited them with more shade and evapotranspiration than the saplings provided. It also ignored that cool paving shifts stored heat into the evening and can push that energy onto adjacent streets. Matching the model to the planting age and the real energy balance, then measuring the heat displaced to neighbouring blocks, would close the gap.

questions.explanation: Models often assume mature canopy and ignore displaced heat, so they overpredict. Measuring real tree age, evapotranspiration and heat pushed to neighbouring blocks reconciles the model with the observed cooling.
questions.hint: Compare the planted trees with the trees the model assumed.

questions.stem: Analysts at the board hear that glacial cycles follow orbital pacing, and they ask why the ice-core signal appears delayed relative to that forcing.

questions.learningObjective: Locate the stage of a retrieval chain that dominates the error

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design an experiment that isolates stored heat in paved surfaces
questions.stem: To isolate stored heat in paving, the board asks for an experimental design that separates it from the other surface energy fluxes.

answer.exemplar: Instrument paved and shaded reference plots with radiometers for surface temperature and an eddy covariance system for sensible heat, and compute net radiation, latent heat and storage as the residual of a closed budget. Repeat the measurement on a paired plot with a reflective coating, on the same wind and solar day, so the change in the storage term can be attributed to the coating rather than to weather.

questions.explanation: Closing the budget over paired plots on the same day isolates storage. The reflective coating gives a controlled contrast, so the change in storage reflects the treatment rather than the weather.
questions.hint: Compare two plots on one day, changing only the surface.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Residence time in the water cycle
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a delayed runoff peak in terms of catchment routing
questions.stem: After a storm the board sees the depot catchment's runoff peak arrive ninety minutes late, and asks what that delay says about the water cycle there.

answer.exemplar: The delay reflects the time the catchment needs to route rainfall to the channel: interception, infiltration and near-surface storage all hold water back before it reaches the drain. A short delay implies a responsive catchment dominated by fast pathways, whereas a long delay points to slow subsurface routing. For a transit planner this matters because a rapid response leaves little time to release stored water before the peak arrives.

questions.explanation: Interception, infiltration and subsurface routing each add delay before water reaches the channel. A short lag means fast pathways, which leaves a depot little time to release stored water before the peak.
questions.hint: Think about which stores the rain must pass through.

questions.learningObjective: Read the lag between an insolation curve and an ice volume curve
questions.stem: A diagram plots summer insolation at 65 degrees north against ice volume, and the board asks how the two curves relate.

options.text: Ice volume tracks summer insolation within the same year with no lag
options.misconception: ignores the lag between forcing and ice response

options.text: Ice volume peaks some millennia after the insolation maximum, with a long lag
Ice volume always moves in step with the opposite winter insolation curve
options.misconception: pins timing to winter forcing without evidence

options.misconception: dismisses insolation as a driver of ice volume

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of whether an old calibration still transfers
questions.stem: The board requests a design testing whether a proxy calibration fitted in the 1980s still holds across the 2000s decade.

answer.exemplar: Split the record into an early block for fitting and a late block for testing, fit the linear relation on the early block alone, then predict the late block from proxy values without refitting. Regress observed on predicted values and report the slope against one, the intercept bias and the residual spread. A slope near one with no systematic bias supports stationarity, while drift in either indicates the mapping no longer transfers.

questions.explanation: Fitting on one block and testing on another reveals whether the relationship transfers, which a combined fit hides. A slope near one with small bias supports stationarity; drift shows it fails.
questions.hint: Never fit and test on the same block of years.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret disagreement between satellite and ground measurements
questions.stem: Ground surveys and satellite retrievals of soil moisture disagree over a rail corridor, and the board asks what that disagreement can and cannot tell you.

answer.exemplar: The disagreement is informative because the two measure different things and at different scales: a satellite senses the top few centimetres over a large footprint, while a probe measures a small volume in depth at one point. Soil heterogeneity, roughness and a timing offset between overpass and probe reading all contribute, so the gap must be interpreted rather than averaged away. It indicates where the retrieval needs work, not that one instrument is useless.

questions.explanation: Satellite and ground instruments differ in scale, depth and timing, so some disagreement is expected and shows where retrievals are weak. Averaging hides that structure.
questions.hint: Ask what each instrument actually measures.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the elevation zone that carries the largest mass loss
questions.stem: A monitoring diagram plots annual mass balance against elevation on one glacier tongue, and the board asks which zone carries the largest annual loss.

options.text: The highest snowfield, because accumulation rises steadily with altitude
options.misconception: assumes higher altitude always means more ice loss

options.text: The lowest tongue, where the equilibrium line sits and melting dominates
The mid-tongue slope, because middle elevations catch the most snowfall
options.misconception: confuses snowfall with the zone of ablation

options.text: The summit ridge, where wind scour removes the deepest snowpack
options.misconception: attributes ablation loss to summit wind scour

questions.explanation: Below the equilibrium line, accumulation fails to replace melting, so loss concentrates on the lower tongue. The upper snowfield gains mass, so deep snow is not where loss is greatest.
questions.hint: Look for the zone where accumulation stops covering melt.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a bench experiment measuring the effect of a transparent layer
questions.stem: For a bench experiment, the board asks how to measure how a single transparent layer changes the longwave and shortwave balance over a soil bed.

answer.exemplar: Set up two identical soil beds, one bare and one covered by a single transparent layer, and place them outdoors under the same sky. Measure incoming and reflected shortwave with a radiometer, measure surface longwave loss with a pyradiometer or an infrared thermometer, and record soil temperature with thermistors at the surface and at depth. Run the pair over several clear and overcast days and compare net radiation and nocturnal cooling rates between the two beds.

questions.explanation: Paired beds under one sky remove weather differences, so changes in net radiation or nocturnal cooling belong to the layer. Repeating over clear and overcast days tests the cover when energy input falls.
questions.hint: Use two identical beds and swap only the cover.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a small insolation change can produce a large ice response
questions.stem: Small changes in summer insolation can drive large changes in ice-sheet mass, and the board asks how that amplification works.

answer.exemplar: Ice sheets are slow, so a small persistent forcing is integrated over centuries rather than answered immediately. Once accumulation starts to exceed melting in a region, that region gains mass, and because ice flow spreads the surplus, added mass can suppress further melting elsewhere through the albedo feedback and reduce sea level, which alters the amount of ocean heat reaching the ice margins. The system therefore responds to a small forcing with a large and slow cumulative change.

questions.explanation: A slow system integrates small persistent forcing over centuries, and the feedback through albedo and ice flow amplifies the initial change. That is why a modest insolation shift can produce a large, slow shift in mass.
questions.hint: Think about feedbacks, not only the initial forcing.

questions.learningObjective: Design a study separating cooling from displacement to neighbouring streets
questions.stem: Studying spillover needs a design that shows whether a cool-pavement pilot lowered temperatures or merely shifted them to neighbouring streets.

answer.exemplar: Treat the pilot area and a matched control neighbourhood as paired units, and monitor surface and air temperature at a dense network of sites in both, including a ring of sensors just outside the treated boundary. Compare the pilot minus control difference before and after the intervention in the treated area, and check whether any rise appears in the ring of sites nearest the boundary. A fall inside with a rise at the boundary indicates displacement rather than a net benefit.

questions.explanation: Sensors only inside the treated area cannot separate cooling from displacement, so the design needs control sites and boundary sensors. A fall inside with a rise outside shows heat moved.
questions.hint: Include sensors just outside the treated boundary.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why two teams may report different glacier retreat rates

answer.exemplar: The teams likely differ in what they call the terminus, how often they visit, and whether they use a handheld global positioning receiver or a fixed stake network. questions.explanation: Teams differ in how they define the terminus and which instrument they use, and each difference changes the rate. A shared definition and benchmark network separate real from method effects.
questions.hint: Compare definitions and instruments before doubting the data.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a systematic bias in an out-of-period prediction
questions.stem: A calibration built on 1960-1990 data predicts 1991-2020 values that sit 1.8 mm low on average, and the board asks what this indicates.

options.text: The relationship has drifted, so the calibration needs updating or a covariate
The proxy has stopped working entirely and should be discarded at once
options.misconception: generalises a small bias into total proxy failure

options.text: The measurements are exact, so the offset must come from rounding of the index
options.misconception: blames rounding rather than a physical drift

options.text: The bias is negligible because 1.8 mm falls inside normal annual rainfall range
options.misconception: treats a systematic bias as ordinary variability

questions.explanation: A consistent low bias across two decades is drift, not scatter, so the old mapping is biased. Updating the fit or adding a covariate fixes it; rounding cannot explain a systematic offset.
questions.hint: A persistent offset is drift, not random scatter.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Place quality screening correctly in a validation workflow
questions.stem: A validation flowchart runs clear-sky screening, cloud masking and then comparison with ground stations, and the board asks where screening must sit.

options.text: Screening must precede the comparison so that only valid pixels reach validation
Screening must come last, so every pixel is compared before any are removed
options.misconception: puts quality control after the comparison step

options.text: Screening is optional, since cloud-affected pixels average out over a season
options.misconception: believes biased pixels cancel out when averaged

options.text: Screening must apply only to ground stations and never to satellite pixels
options.misconception: applies quality control to the wrong dataset

questions.explanation: Quality control must come first, otherwise invalid pixels bias the comparison statistics. Seasonal averaging does not rescue it, because cloud-affected errors are systematic rather than random.
questions.hint: Filter the data before you compare it.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a campaign measuring the full surface energy balance seasonally
questions.stem: Measuring the full budget needs a campaign that covers the surface energy balance of a bus depot roof over a full seasonal cycle.

answer.exemplar: Mount an eddy covariance system on a mast above the depot roof to measure sensible heat, pair it with a scintillometer or lysimeter for the latent term, and a net radiometer for net radiation, with soil heat flux plates, a rain gauge and thermistors for the storage term and ground conditions. Log at high frequency through a full year so that seasonal shifts in albedo, moisture and vegetation are captured, and derive the storage flux as the residual that closes the budget.

questions.explanation: A full seasonal cycle needs every term measured over months, not weeks, because albedo and moisture change with season. Deriving storage as the residual turns closure into a real check.
questions.hint: Measure continuously for a year, not for a fortnight.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Residence time in the water cycle
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a long theoretical residence time coexists with rapid flooding
questions.stem: Flood risk rises when a shallow detention basin overflows, and the board asks how a long theoretical residence time can coexist with that.

answer.exemplar: Residence time describes the average turnover of stored water, while the flood peak depends on how fast water can reach the outlet. If the basin's storage is small and its outflow capacity is limited, water can remain for a long average time yet still exceed the available capacity in a single storm. The flood is therefore set by peak inflow and outflow capacity, whereas residence time reflects the long-run balance between the two.

questions.explanation: Residence time describes average turnover, while a flood depends on how fast water reaches the outlet and how much it can carry. A long average residence does not prevent overloading at peak inflow.
questions.hint: Separate long-run average from a single storm peak.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Average two equal-sized sets of block temperature measurements
questions.stem: After the intervention, six of twelve monitored blocks averaged 35.2 °C and the other six averaged 39.8 °C; what is the mean across all twelve blocks?
questions.explanation: The groups are the same size, so the mean is the average of the group means: 35.2 plus 39.8 is 75.0, and half of that is 37.5 °C. Summing block by block agrees.
questions.hint: Equal groups mean the overall mean is the mean of means.

questions.learningObjective: Justify using a network of stakes rather than a single stake
questions.stem: Stake networks outperform a single stake near the snout, and the board asks why that is the better design.

options.text: A single stake cannot detect melting, so only networks can find ablation
options.misconception: says one stake cannot detect ablation at all

options.text: Stake networks are required for insurance on the rail line below
options.misconception: invents an insurance requirement for monitoring

options.text: A spread of stakes samples the elevation and aspect range where melt varies
Stake networks shorten travel time between successive measurement points
options.misconception: confuses logistical convenience with scientific value

questions.explanation: Melting varies with elevation, aspect and snow depth, so one stake reports a single point rather than the range. A network spread across the tongue integrates those varying conditions properly.
questions.hint: One point cannot describe a whole tongue.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a covered surface stays warmer at night
questions.stem: A covered walkway stays 4.5 °C warmer at night than an uncovered one, and the board asks which process explains the difference.

options.text: The cover increases the incoming shortwave radiation reaching the ground
options.misconception: believes shortwave radiation arrives at night

options.text: The cover raises the albedo of the paving underneath it
options.misconception: confuses cover reflectivity with surface albedo

options.text: The cover blocks rainfall so the surface stays drier through the night
options.misconception: credits the cover with blocking rainfall

options.text: The cover suppresses radiative cooling, so less heat leaves the surface overnight

questions.explanation: Night cooling is dominated by longwave emission, and a cover blocks part of that path, so the surface stays warmer. The cover adds no sunlight at night and leaves the paving's albedo unchanged.
questions.hint: Think about which loss the cover blocks after sunset.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the event marked by a step in the sea level record
questions.stem: A curve chart plots global sea level against time with a stepped rise about 20,000 years ago, and the board asks what the step marks.

options.text: The start of Northern Hemisphere deglaciation after the last glacial maximum
The end of the last interglacial, when ice sheets began to grow again
options.misconception: reverses the sign of the deglaciation event

options.text: A volcanic eruption that darkened skies for several centuries
options.misconception: invents a volcanic cause for a sea level step

options.text: The arrival of agriculture, which changed global land use abruptly
options.misconception: links a climate signal to a human land-use change

questions.explanation: A step of this size and timing matches the rapid loss of ice sheets after the last glacial maximum, which poured water into the ocean. Volcanic or land-use causes do not fit its shape.
questions.hint: Ask which ice event added water to the ocean.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of the variance a proxy explains
questions.stem: Explaining how much variance a proxy holds requires a design that measures the explained variance directly.

answer.exemplar: Pair proxy values with independent observations of the target variable over the longest overlapping period available, then fit the relationship and report the coefficient of determination alongside the slope. Cross-validate by withholding blocks of years and predicting them from the fitted relation, because an in-sample value of r squared can look strong while the relation fails out of sample. Compare the skill against a simple baseline such as the long-term mean.

questions.explanation: Explained variance must be judged on data not used in fitting, otherwise skill looks better than it is. Blocked cross-validation against a baseline shows whether the proxy adds real information.
questions.hint: Test the relation on years you did not fit it with.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why summer validation cannot support winter snow estimates
questions.stem: Summer-only validation cannot support winter snow estimates, and the board asks why the evidence does not transfer.

answer.exemplar: Winter snow changes everything the retrieval depends on: the surface is bright and cold, the sun angle is low, snow and cloud are hard to separate in the visible, and melt can leave patchy ground that looks like snow from above. A product validated on moist summer vegetation therefore says little about snow conditions, and its error distribution was estimated in a regime that never occurs in winter. Winter-specific validation and separate error statistics are needed.

questions.explanation: Validation statistics describe the conditions during validation, so summer results do not describe winter snow. Snow changes reflectance, illumination and the snow-to-cloud signal, so errors need fresh estimates.
questions.hint: Ask whether the validation conditions match the target use.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Compute the Bowen ratio from sensible and latent heat fluxes
questions.stem: Over a midday hour the sensible heat flux is 90 W/m² and the latent heat flux is 150 W/m²; what is the Bowen ratio for that interval?
questions.explanation: The Bowen ratio is sensible flux over latent flux, so 90 divided by 150 is 0.6. Reversing the ratio gives 1.67 and wrongly implies most energy went into evaporation.
questions.hint: Divide sensible flux by latent flux.

questions.topic: Residence time in the water cycle
questions.learningObjective: Define atmospheric residence time of water
questions.stem: Atmospheric residence describes the average time water stays airborne, and the board asks which definition applies.

options.text: The time a single raindrop spends inside one cloud before it falls
options.misconception: confuses atmospheric residence with one cloud

options.text: The average delay between evaporation and the next local rainfall event
options.misconception: reduces atmospheric residence to a local cycle

options.text: The time groundwater stays underground before discharging into rivers
options.misconception: borrows groundwater residence for the atmosphere

options.text: The average time water remains airborne before returning to the surface

questions.explanation: Atmospheric residence time is the average lifetime of water in the atmosphere, set by precipitation, evaporation and storage. Confining it to one cloud or one local shower describes a shorter cycle.
questions.hint: Think about the whole atmospheric store, not one cloud.

questions.learningObjective: Weigh a summer cooling benefit against a winter heating cost
questions.stem: Cool roofs cut summer rooftop temperatures by 6 °C but winter heating demand rose 4%, and the board asks how to weigh the trade-off.

options.text: The net benefit depends on the local cost of summer cooling against winter heating
The intervention failed, because any winter increase cancels the summer gain
options.misconception: lets one effect wipe out the other entirely

options.text: The intervention succeeded, because lower temperatures always reduce costs
options.misconception: assumes lower temperature always means lower cost

options.text: Only the summer change matters, since winter heating is optional locally
options.misconception: dismisses winter heating demand as irrelevant

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Read a mass balance band below the zero line
questions.stem: A diagram plots annual mass balance against distance from the snout and shows a narrow band of retreating flowlines.

options.text: Only the upper accumulation zone is retreating, so the snout stays stable
options.misconception: ignores the retreat signal near the snout

options.text: The glacier advances at the snout while retreating far upstream
options.misconception: reverses the retreat direction along the tongue

options.text: The band shows yearly noise only, with no underlying trend
options.misconception: dismisses a consistent multi-year signal as noise

options.text: The band sits below the zero line, so the terminus is losing mass

questions.explanation: A narrow band below zero means every flowline sampled is losing mass year on year, not fluctuating. The terminus is therefore retreating, and calling the pattern noise ignores that consistency.
questions.hint: A band below the zero line means net loss.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a matched comparison of single and double layer covers
questions.stem: Comparing covers directly requires a matched design for a single layer against a double layer over the same soil bed.

answer.exemplar: Use three soil beds with identical moisture and surface condition, keeping one bare, one under a single transparent layer and one under two separated layers with a gap for insulating air. Log incoming shortwave, net longwave loss and soil temperature at the surface and 5 cm depth over several clear nights and days, then compare nocturnal cooling rates and daytime soil warming between the three beds. The double layer should show stronger night-time retention and slightly lower daytime light gain.

questions.explanation: Matching soil moisture and surface isolates the cover as the only variable, and the air gap separates a double cover from a single one. Comparing the same measures shows where the extra layer helps.
questions.hint: Keep the soil and the weather identical between beds.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why deglaciation timing lags the insolation maximum
questions.stem: Deglaciation timing does not match the timing of maximum summer insolation, and the board asks why the two records diverge.

answer.exemplar: The maximum in summer insolation at high northern latitudes marks when the forcing is strongest, but the ice sheet responds to an integrated energy budget rather than to a single season. Termination begins where the summer warmth and the snowfall changes together cross a threshold, and once started, thicker, softer ice and rising ocean levels accelerate the loss in ways the insolation curve alone does not show. The response therefore runs late and can appear abrupt compared with the smooth forcing curve.

questions.explanation: The sheet responds to an integrated budget rather than a single peak, so the response runs late. Positive feedbacks then make the change look abrupt beside the smooth insolation curve, as expected.
questions.hint: Compare a forcing curve with an integrated response.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose a failure of surface energy budget closure
questions.stem: Measured fluxes show net radiation of 340 W/m², latent 120, sensible 70 and storage 60 W/m², and the board asks what the imbalance shows.

options.text: The budget is unbalanced, so the flux data should be discarded entirely
options.misconception: discards data instead of diagnosing the closure gap

options.text: The budget misses 90 W/m², so a term such as advection is unaccounted for
The budget closes exactly, because net radiation always equals the other three
options.misconception: assumes the surface budget always closes

options.text: The gap is negligible, since 90 W/m² is within the noise of every sensor
options.misconception: waves away a large closure gap as noise

questions.explanation: The three fluxes sum to 250 W/m² against 340 W/m² of net radiation, leaving 90 W/m² unaccounted for. The gap points to a missing term such as advection or a measurement error.
questions.hint: Add the three fluxes and compare with net radiation.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Residence time in the water cycle
questions.learningObjective: Rank the turnover times of soil, aquifer and river stores
questions.stem: A catchment schematic shows a soil column, a shallow aquifer and a river fed by both, and the board asks which store turns over fastest.

options.text: The soil column, because it receives rainfall on every wet day
options.misconception: equates frequent wetting with rapid turnover

options.text: The deep aquifer, because groundwater sits under pressure down there
options.misconception: links pressure to rapid turnover

options.text: The river, because its store is small and outflow responds quickly
All three stores turn over equally, since water moves between them
options.misconception: ignores the large differences in store size

questions.explanation: Turnover time is store over flux, and the river holds less water and passes it through quickly, so its residence time is the shortest. The aquifer stores water far longer than the river does.
questions.hint: Turnover is the store divided by the flow through it.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a study separating canopy from resurfacing effects
questions.stem: Separating canopy from resurfacing needs a design that isolates the effect of new tree planting from the new carriageway surface.

answer.exemplar: Use a factorial layout with four plots: untreated, trees only, new surfacing only, and both treatments together, each plot large enough to avoid the shading of a neighbouring plot. Hold traffic, bus spacing and irrigation constant, measure surface and canopy temperature along transects crossing each plot on the same days, and compare the single-treatment plots against the untreated plot to obtain each effect separately. The combined plot then tests whether the two measures interfere with one another.

questions.explanation: A factorial layout separates the effects, because single-treatment plots show each alone while the combined plot reveals interaction. Holding traffic and irrigation constant excludes other causes.
questions.hint: Use untreated, one treatment each, and both together.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain what automatic weather stations cannot tell a monitoring programme
questions.stem: Weather stations alone cannot replace stake surveys in a glacier monitoring programme, and the board asks what the instruments miss.

answer.exemplar: A weather station measures atmosphere and snow depth at one point, which is enough to model melt at that point but not to describe where the ice actually is. Stakes and global positioning surveys locate the surface itself, so they capture the advance, retreat, thinning and crevasse patterns that drive the loss. The station explains why melt happens; the stakes show what the glacier is doing. A programme using only the station can forecast runoff accurately while missing a terminus that has retreated.

questions.explanation: A weather station explains why melt occurs at its location but cannot show where the ice lies. Stakes and positioning surveys capture thinning and retreat, so both types are needed for a reliable programme.
questions.hint: One measures the weather, the other measures the ice.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the longwave fraction passing through a cover
questions.stem: Outgoing longwave loss from a covered surface is 380 W/m² and the cover blocks 40% of it; how much longwave is lost through the cover?
questions.explanation: The blocked share is 380 times 0.40, which is 152 W/m², so 228 W/m² escapes through the cover. Confusing blocked with remaining shares reverses the answer.
questions.hint: Blocked energy is the fraction times the total.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why glacial cycles recur on the same orbital rhythm
questions.stem: Ice core records repeat both glacial and interglacial states on roughly the same orbital rhythm, and the board asks why.

options.text: Because orbital forcing is the only influence on ice volume in any model
options.misconception: treats orbital forcing as the sole influence without caveat

options.text: Because random variations in cosmic dust drive the alternating states
options.misconception: invents a random dust mechanism

options.text: Because the forcing modulates the energy balance, and the ice responds each time
Because the deep ocean stores every forcing and releases it for millennia
options.misconception: hands all pacing to the ocean without evidence

questions.explanation: Orbital forcing repeatedly changes the seasonal energy balance and ice responds each time, so the rhythm recurs. Random dust would not repeat on schedule, and the ocean only moderates the response.
questions.hint: A repeating rhythm points to a repeating driver.

questions.learningObjective: Use a sediment proxy as an indicator rather than a direct measurement
questions.stem: A sediment core proxy records dry years when the inflow to a reservoir is low, and the board asks how this proxy should be used.

options.text: Treat it as an indicator of inflow and check it against gauge records before use
Treat it as a direct measurement of reservoir volume in each year
options.misconception: equates an index with a physical volume

options.text: Ignore it, since proxies only record temperature and never water balance
options.misconception: restricts proxies to temperature records

options.text: Convert it to volume by multiplying by the reservoir's surface area
options.misconception: applies a meaningless area conversion

questions.explanation: An index records a relative condition, so it can flag low-inflow years but cannot supply a volume alone. Gauge records test the link; multiplying by surface area invents a quantity.
questions.hint: An index indicates; it does not measure volumes.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Choose the best validation target surface from a set of candidates
questions.stem: A diagram shows a satellite passing over a road, a tree canopy and a glass roof, and the board asks which surface offers the best validation target.

options.text: The glass roof, because it has the lowest surface temperature of the three
options.misconception: picks a target for low temperature rather than stability

options.text: The tree canopy, because it provides a large, stable and well-mixed target
The road, because asphalt is homogeneous and easy to sample at any hour

options.text: The moving satellite itself, since it sees every surface equally well
options.misconception: treats the instrument as its own validation target

questions.explanation: A good target must fill the footprint, be uniform enough to predict the sensor's view and be stable enough to compare times. Canopy meets these better than asphalt or glass.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a measurement of the albedo of a new carriageway surface
questions.stem: Estimating albedo requires a paired design that measures the reflectance of a new light-coloured carriageway accurately.

answer.exemplar: Use a hemispherical reflectance sensor or a calibrated spectrometer to measure incoming and reflected shortwave over sample patches of the new surface and of the old surface under identical sky conditions, in both dry and wet states and at several sun angles. Repeat the measurement across the carriageway to capture variability from joints, markings and wear, and report the reflectance with its spread rather than a single average, since the road surface changes with age.

questions.explanation: Albedo is reflected over incoming shortwave, so both must be measured on the same patch under one sky. Sampling the carriageway dry and wet captures variability one reading would miss.
questions.hint: Measure incoming and reflected light on the same patch.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Residence time in the water cycle
questions.learningObjective: Explain how fast turnover worsens downstream flooding
questions.stem: Quick turnover in a rapid-response catchment makes downstream flooding worse, and the board asks how.

answer.exemplar: A short residence time means most of the rain reaches the channel within minutes rather than hours, so a storm's runoff arrives as one concentrated peak instead of being spread out. The channel therefore carries a much higher flow than a slower catchment with the same total rainfall, and any storage that could absorb part of the peak has not had time to fill. Slowing the response by encouraging infiltration and by holding water in the upper catchment flattens the same peak.

questions.explanation: Fast routing concentrates a storm's runoff into one peak instead of spreading it over hours, so the channel carries a higher flow for the same rain. Storage cannot fill in time, and the peak arrives early.
questions.hint: Fast water arrives together rather than spread out.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Compute a treatment effect from a negative control change
questions.stem: Treated blocks in a pilot cooled by 2.4 °C while control blocks warmed by 0.6 °C; what is the treatment effect on temperature change?
questions.explanation: The effect is the treated change minus the control change: 2.4 minus negative 0.6 gives 3.0 °C. Adding magnitudes gives 1.8 °C and ignores the control's direction.
questions.hint: Subtract the control change from the treated change.
